To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brothers' differential learning outcomes were the result of the combined effects of their individual agency and their differential accumulation and utilization of different forms of social capital that were available to them.

(1) the two brothers' different social capital and individual agency influenced their educational outcomes, (2) social capital and individual family agency were not the only influences, (3) each brother's social capital and individual educational agency was influenced by the family, and (4) the family's social capital and family agency were not only the result of individual family members' experiences and actions, but were also shaped by the social context.
the differential social and educational capital available to each of the brothers, as a result of their different communities of practice, was an influential factor in their learning outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding how the social capital of the family, in the form of cultural capital and social support, is transformed through the agency of the student and the role of the mentor in this transformation.
the role social class, gender and family influence play in the construction of learning identities and how this influences working-class students' learning outcomes.

the role social and cultural capital play in the lives of students, particularly in the lives of working-class boys and the ways in which these resources can be mobilized to facilitate or impede the acquisition and utilization of educational knowledge
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the two boys' differential learning outcomes were not solely a result of their family's social class position, but were the result of the boys' differential accumulation of social capital, which in turn was influenced by a number of factors, including the brothers' differential individual agency and their differential access to the social capital of their parents.
the differential learning identities of two brothers from the same family can be explained by the brothers' differential accumulation and utilization of social capital.
this research has demonstrated how the differential social capital and individual agency of two white babyboomer brothers from a working-class family affected the learning outcomes of each brother.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brothers' differential learning outcomes were the product of their individual agency and social capital accumulation and utilization.
the two brothers' learning identities were shaped by the social capital they accrued from their family and community.
the social capital of a family member is not fixed and that a student's social identity can be transformed by the individual's agency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
while family and community social capital are important, they may not be as important as previously thought in understanding the learning trajectories of working-class students.
social capital and agency are inextricably linked and that the social capital of the individual student is the best means of predicting learning outcomes. (Author abstract)
